content_voiceover: This slide quantifies the relative risk of inhibitor development associated with different F8 genotype mutation classes, using inversions as the reference at one-fold risk. Large deletions greater than two hundred base pairs carry an inhibitor prevalence of thirty-eight percent, which translates to a three point six fold increased risk relative to inversions. Nonsense mutations show thirty-six percent prevalence and a one point four fold relative risk. Inversions themselves, the classic intron 22 or intron 1 inversions, serve as the baseline at twenty percent prevalence and one-fold risk. Small deletions, eighty-six base pairs or less, carry fourteen percent prevalence and a lower zero point five fold relative risk. And missense mutations, the mildest genetic lesion, carry only seven percent prevalence and zero point three fold relative risk. The overall pattern to remember is that mutations causing complete absence of factor eight protein, large deletions and nonsense mutations, drive the highest inhibitor risk, because the immune system has never been tolerized to any factor eight protein, whereas missense mutations, which still produce a full-length but dysfunctional protein, carry the lowest risk because partial self-tolerance exists.
keypoints: Large deletions carry the highest inhibitor risk, 3.6-fold relative to inversions
Missense mutations carry the lowest risk, 0.3-fold, due to partial immune tolerance
Null mutation types, large deletions and nonsense mutations, predict highest inhibitor incidence
keypoint_voiceover: Key points to remember. Large deletions carry the highest relative risk of inhibitor development, three point six fold compared to inversions. Nonsense mutations carry a smaller but still elevated one point four fold risk. Missense mutations carry the lowest risk, only zero point three fold, because some tolerizing factor eight protein is still produced. The unifying concept is that null mutations, ones that produce no factor eight protein at all, drive the highest inhibitor incidence.
